prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Federal Data Terminations Tracker

The most policy-relevant, verified source of federal datasets terminated since January 2025.

Have a termination or removal to add? Contact us at removals@dataindex.us.

Read more about the methodology and why quantifying data terminations is so challenging in this Federation of American Scientists blogpost. To learn more about the Federal Data Terminations Tracker, watch our briefing.

Last updated: August 17, 2026.

Looking for the Dearly Departed Datasets tracker published in October 2025? View the archive →

Download CSV

Showing all 375 entries

Datasets Terminated 38

No entries in this section match your filters.

Energy

International Energy Outlook (IEO)

Agency: EIA

EIA's long-range projections of world energy production, consumption, and prices out to mid-century.

Caveats: A biennial modeling report rather than a data collection. The 2023 edition remains the most recent; EIA dropped the 2025 edition following staff losses and indicated at the time that it might publish later. No termination notice has been issued, so Date terminated is left blank.

Sources

  • The Nation's Data at Risk: Energy Information Administration – American Statistical Association

Federal workforce

Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS)

Agency: OPM

OPM's annual survey of the federal workforce, the government-wide measure of how employees viewed their jobs, leaders, and agencies.

Caveats: A successor survey is planned, but as a short common form each agency runs itself rather than OPM's standardized government-wide survey. Some previous data was redacted for reports 2012-2024. See page 11,12. There were also removals of "DEI related questions"

Sources

  • Agency Information Collection Request: Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (91 FR 40599) – Federal Register Notice
  • 2025 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey and Compliance with Recent Executive Orders (OPM memo, archived) – Wayback Machine
  • OPM will forego FEVS in 2025, despite law requiring it – Government Executive
  • Archived copy (Wayback Machine)

International development

Development Data Library (DDL)

Agency: USAID

USAID's public library of the data produced by the projects and research it funded.

Caveats: The evidence is a pair of archived captures showing the portal live on January 16, 2025 and redirecting to a sign-in page by February 1 - a loss of public access rather than a documented decision to destroy the holdings. Date terminated reflects the first capture showing access closed. Data is available on the University of Michigan's data lumos platform per june data sharing agreement

Sources

  • USAID Development Data Library (archived 2025-01-16, live) – Wayback Machine
  • USAID Development Data Library (archived 2025-02-01, redirect to sign-in) – Wayback Machine
  • USAID website goes dark amid Trump administration's freeze on foreign aid worldwide – Associated Press via PBS NewsHour

Disasters

Future Risk Index

Agency: FEMA

FEMA's interactive map projecting how much money climate-driven disasters would cost each U.S. county in the decades ahead.

Caveats: This is a model, not primary data, but it is an important product to come from the US Government instead of outside groups.

Sources

  • FEMA Removed Future Risk Index – Harvard Law School Environmental & Energy Law Program
  • The online climate tool that Trump removed, but data scientists have now rebuilt – Geographical (Royal Geographical Society)
  • fulton-ring/nri-future-risk – Fulton Ring (GitHub rebuild)
  • Archived copy (Wayback Machine)

Health

Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS)

Agency: USAID

USAID-funded household surveys that tracked health, fertility, and nutrition in more than 90 low- and middle-income countries for four decades.

Caveats: Other funders have stepped in to complete current rounds and make sure data are available historically.

Sources

  • The End of the DHS Program and the Future of Gender Data: What's at Stake – UN Women
  • The DHS Program – USAID program site

Demographics

Community Resilience Estimates Equity Supplement

Agency: CENSUS

Census product that layered income inequality and other equity measures onto its community resilience estimates for local areas.

Caveats: The evidence is a pair of archived captures showing the page live on February 2, 2025 and returning a 404 the following day. No discontinuation notice has been located; what is documented is removal from public access. Date terminated reflects the first capture returning 404.

Sources

  • Community Resilience Estimates Equity Supplement (archived 2025-02-02, live) – Wayback Machine
  • U.S. Census Bureau: Page not found (archived 2025-02-03) – Wayback Machine
  • Support Dearly Departed Datasets – Data Rescue Project

Agriculture

NASS State-Specific Reports

Agency: USDA

Crop and livestock reports tailored to individual states, published by NASS's state field offices.

Caveats: The underlying data are still collected and available through NASS's Quick Stats database; what ended is the state-report format. NASS has plans to force relocation of their employees to Saint Louis. There is a major loss of staff is expected. A lawsuit has blocked the reorganization until October 2nd, 2026 with a hearing set for September 29th, 2026

Sources

  • NASS to End State-Specific Reports – Red River Farm Network

Health

Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS)

Agency: CDC

CDC and state health department survey of new mothers about their experiences before, during, and after pregnancy.

Caveats: Data collection is continuing as states fund it, standardized weighting and publication at the national level has ceased. The states no longer participating in prams are Idaho, California, Ohio, and North Carolina These states conduct their own survey

Sources

  • Proposed Data Collection Submitted for Public Comment and Recommendations (90 FR 52666, PRAMS) – Federal Register Notice
  • Gold-standard maternal mortality database in limbo as CDC staff placed on leave – STAT News
  • The Landscape of Major Federal Health Survey Data Releases in 2025 – SHADAC
  • Archived copy (Wayback Machine)

Education

Progress in International Reading Literacy Study 2026 (U.S. participation) (PIRLS)

Agency: ED

International assessment of fourth-grade reading comprehension; the United States is absent from the 2026 cycle after participating in every round since 2001.

Caveats: The United States has participated in every PIRLS cycle since 2001 and does not appear on IEA's published participant list for 2026, which IEA gives as 64 education systems. The contract covering PIRLS, PIAAC, and PISA was terminated for convenience on February 12, 2025 and reinstated on March 6, 2025 in a modification titled for the international assessment program; no record reinstating the PIRLS scope has been located. NCES has issued no notice cancelling U.S. participation and we have received no statement from the Department — this entry records absence from the participant list, not an announced withdrawal. Date terminated reflects the reinstatement modification that excluded PIRLS. All prior PIRLS rounds remain available.

Sources

  • PIRLS 2026 participants – IEA
  • PIRLS Schedule and Plans – NCES program page

Education

High School and Beyond 2022 first follow-up (HS&B:22)

Agency: ED

Longitudinal study of a national cohort of ninth-graders; the base year was collected and the planned spring 2026 follow-up was cancelled.

Caveats: The base-year ninth-grade data were released in DataLab on July 20, 2026 and remain available. What ended is the spring 2026 follow-up: the task order carrying it was terminated for convenience on February 10, 2025 and funding was deobligated on April 25, 2025. Date terminated reflects the contract termination. Termination for convenience is a routine federal contracting mechanism exercised at the government's election and does not indicate any deficiency in contractor performance.

I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Survey of Children's Health (NSCH)
Description: The National Survey of Children's Health is a household survey that produces national and state-level data on the physical and emotional health of children 0 - 17 years old in the United States. The survey collects information related to the health and well-being of children, including access to and use of health care, family interactions, parental health, school and after-school experiences, and neighborhood characteristics.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively. Let me start with several parallel searches covering the publisher, authority/mandate, history, and usage.I have strong foundational material. Now let me dig into data products, methodology, access tools, and current status.I have one gap to close — the confidentiality/privacy protections. Let me fetch the HRSA participant FAQ page directly.# The National Survey of Children's Health (NSCH): A Complete Research Report

## 0. Verification of the Supplied Description

The description you provided is **verbatim accurate** — it matches the official "What is the NSCH?" wording in the Census Bureau's annual NSCH FAQs (e.g., the 2025 Methodology and Data User FAQs). The URL is correct as well; note that the canonical form is `https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch.html`. One nuance worth adding to any catalog record: the Census Bureau is the *data collector and publisher*, but the survey is *sponsored and primarily funded* by HRSA's Maternal and Child Health Bureau (MCHB) within HHS. Your description omits this dual-agency structure, which is essential to understanding the dataset's authority, funding, and future.

---

## 1. Who Publishes It (Stewardship and Actors)

The NSCH has an unusually multi-agency stewardship structure:

| Role | Actor |
|---|---|
| **Sponsor / primary funder / content owner** | HRSA Maternal and Child Health Bureau (MCHB), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services |
| **Data collector & public data producer** | U.S. Census Bureau (Associate Director for Demographic Programs), under interagency agreement |
| **Supplementary funders** | CDC (NCBDDD, NCCDPHP, NCEH divisions) and USDA Food and Nutrition Service (2025); CDC funded young-child (0–5) oversamples in 2021–2023; nine states (CA, CO, NE, NY, OH, OR, PA, TN, WI) plus metro Atlanta have purchased oversamples |
| **Dissemination partner** | The Child and Adolescent Health Measurement Initiative (CAHMI) operates the **Data Resource Center for Child and Adolescent Health (DRC)** at childhealthdata.org / nschdata.org, which turns NSCH microdata into prebuilt indicators and datasets |
| **Historical steward (pre-2016)** | CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which fielded the original survey via the SLAITS system and still archives the 2001–2012 data |

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

The NSCH operates under a two-statute authority structure, both of which are stated on the survey instrument itself:

1. **Title 13, U.S.C., Section 8(b)** — authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct surveys *on behalf of other federal agencies*. This is the mechanism by which the Census Bureau legally fields the NSCH for HRSA/HHS.
2. **Title 42, U.S.C., Section 701(a)(2)** (Section 501 of the Social Security Act, the Title V authority) — authorizes HHS to collect information for the purpose of understanding the health and well-being of children in the United States.

Supporting statutory/policy framework:

- **Title V Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Services Block Grant** (Social Security Act Title V; 42 U.S.C. §§701–709; permanently authorized by P.L. 74-121). Section 505(a) requires every state to conduct a **statewide needs assessment every five years** as a condition of receiving Title V funds — this is the NSCH's core policy mandate. The NSCH is the data source for **9 of 15 National Performance Measures (NPMs) and 7 of 25 National Outcome Measures (NOMs)** used to evaluate the $850M+/year Title V program, and provides baseline estimates for state five-year needs assessments and **15 child health objectives for Healthy People 2030**.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance**: current OMB Control No. **0607-0990** ("National Survey of Children's Health 2026"), approved with change on June 16, 2026, expiring June 30, 2029; roughly 126,700 responses and ~42,500 burden hours annually. The full ICR history at OMB/reginfo documents a new collection in 2016 followed by annual revision requests — a useful paper trail of every questionnaire change since the redesign.
- **Confidentiality**: the survey instrument carries the standard Census Bureau statistical-use pledge — responses are used only for statistical purposes and cannot be published or used in any way that could identify a household. Participation is voluntary (this is not a mandatory Title 13 enumeration), and the PUFs are heavily de-identified/disclosure-reviewed.

## 3. History

**Phase 1 — SLAITS era (2001–2012).** MCHB sponsored two companion telephone surveys run as modules of CDC/NCHS's State and Local Area Integrated Telephone Survey (SLAITS), using the National Immunization Survey's random-digit-dial landline frame: the **National Survey of Children with Special Health Care Needs (NS-CSHCN)** (2001, 2005–06, 2009–10) and the **NSCH** (2003, 2007, 2011–12). The 2011–12 NSCH collected nearly 96,000 completed interviews in English, Spanish, Mandarin, and other languages. These surveys were the primary source of national *and state-level* child health estimates for Title V reporting.

**Phase 2 — The 2016 redesign.** Declining response rates, the collapse of the landline frame (cell-phone supplementation proved costly and inefficient), and rising costs made the old design unsustainable. In 2015 MCHB **combined the NSCH and NS-CSHCN into a single survey** (retaining the NSCH name and embedding the CSHCN Screener), moved to an **address-based sampling (ABS) frame drawn from the Census Master Address File**, shifted from telephone interviews to **self-administered web and paper questionnaires**, made the survey **annual** (previously every ~4 years), and **transferred collection from NCHS to the Census Bureau**. A national pretest of 16,000 addresses was run in 2015; the redesigned survey has been fielded every year since 2016, with public use files available for 2016–2025.

**Recent events of record:**
- CDC funded oversampling of young children (ages 0–5) in 2021–2023.
- The **October–November 2025 lapse in federal appropriations** (government shutdown) disrupted mailout operations for the 2025 NSCH; closeout was extended from mid-January to March 6, 2026, and an extra $5 incentive mailing was added to compensate.
- The 2026 NSCH ICR was approved in June 2026, indicating the program remains active, with ongoing response-rate experiments (incentive envelope tests, web-partial follow-ups).

**Critical comparability break**: because the mode, frame, and content changed fundamentally in 2016, **the Census Bureau explicitly warns against trending pre-2016 vs. post-2016 estimates**. Treat them as two different series. Also note the Census Bureau re-issued weights for 2016–2019 files, and DRC's pre-built indicator datasets for those years were *not* all updated — a known trap for anyone reproducing older analyses.

## 4. Methodology and Data Design (a data scientist's view)

Based on the 2023 cycle (representative of the current design):

- **Frame & stratification**: ~385,000 addresses sampled from the Census Master Address File, stratified by probability of child presence derived from administrative records (strata 1a/1b: addresses linked to children, with young children sampled at the highest rate; 2a: probable; 2b: low-probability, excluded).
- **Two-phase design**: (1) a **household screener** identifying children 0–17 and administering the CSHCN Screener; (2) an age-specific **topical questionnaire** (0–5, 6–11, 12–17) about one randomly selected child, completed by a **parent or guardian**.
- **Oversampling**: children with special health care needs (80%) and ages 0–5 (60%), to compensate for underrepresentation.
- **Output volume (2023)**: 70,187 children reported on completed screeners; **55,162 completed topical questionnaires** (state range: 710–4,696); roughly 15,000 households with children did not return a sufficient topical questionnaire.
- **Response rates (2023)**: weighted screener completion 41.9%; topical completion 27.1%; interview completion 76.3%; **overall weighted response rate 35.8%** — typical of the modern household-survey environment, and mitigated by published nonresponse bias analyses.
- **Weighting**: the topical file carries a final child weight (**FWC**); screener files carry child (C_FWS) and household (FWH) weights. Weighting applies base weights × screener nonresponse adjustment × child-listing subsampling factor × within-household subsampling factor × topical nonresponse adjustment × raking to ACS demographic controls (state × poverty ratio, household size, education, race/ethnicity, age group), with trimming. Variance estimation guidance and replicate-based methods are documented in each year's Source and Accuracy Statement — read it before computing standard errors; survey procedures (Stata `svy`, R `survey`) are required, not optional.
- **Analytic guidance**: single-year files support national estimates; **two-year combined files** are the recommended basis for state-level estimates and small subgroups. HRSA recommends suppressing estimates with unweighted denominators below 30 and flagging results where the 95% CI exceeds 20 percentage points or 1.2× the estimate (RSE > 30%). Small populations (e.g., American Indian/Alaska Native children) and rare state-level outcomes (e.g., autism among CSHCN adolescents in one state) are known weak spots.

**Content domains**: physical health; emotional/mental/behavioral health; special health care needs; health insurance; access to and quality of health care (medical home); developmental screening; family interactions and structure; parental health; school and after-school experiences; neighborhood characteristics; "Healthy and Ready to Learn" school-readiness items; food security and nutrition. Content evolves annually (e.g., 2025 added items on asthma attacks, fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, hours of non-parental care, and ADHD medication shortages; 2026 revisions documented in the OMB package) — check the year-by-year content-change guides before pooling.

## 5. Data Products and Access Channels

1. **Census Bureau PUFs** (free, public, no license): screener file + child-level topical file per year, in **SAS and Stata formats**, with codebooks, questionnaires (in English and Spanish), methodology reports, FAQs, Source & Accuracy Statements, and nonresponse bias analyses. Available for 2016–2025.
2. **CAHMI/DRC Interactive Data Query** (childhealthdata.org / nschdata.org): point-and-click access to 300+ pre-constructed indicators, Title V NPMs/NOMs, maps, and state comparison tables for all 50 states + DC, by demographic subgroups — the primary access route for non-technical users.
3. **DRC Indicator Datasets**: enhanced, fully labeled SAS/SPSS/Stata/CSV files containing all PUF variables plus dozens of constructed measures and subpopulation variables, available free after a data user agreement (a tracking mechanism, not a fee).
4. **Pre-2016 legacy data**: archived at CDC NCHS (SLAITS program pages) and mirrored through the DRC — an important preservation dependency, since NCHS hosts the entire 2001–2012 SLAITS-era NSCH and NS-CSHCN archive.

## 6. Typical Users

- **State Title V MCH programs** — the anchor user community: five-year needs assessments, annual reporting, and NPM selection (most commonly NPM-11 Medical Home, selected by 44 states, and NPM-6 Developmental Screening, selected by 40 states).
- **Federal policymakers** — HRSA for Title V accountability and reports to Congress; CDC and USDA divisions that co-fund content modules; Healthy People 2030 tracking.
- **Researchers** — the largest national/state survey of child health, widely used in pediatrics, health services, and child-development literature.
- **Child health advocates, community organizations, educators, journalists, and families** — primarily via the DRC's easy-access query tools.
- **State/local health departments** purchasing oversamples for sub-state precision.

## 7. Benefits to the Public

The NSCH is, by HRSA's own characterization, **the only national and state-level survey on the health and well-being of children, their families, and their communities**, and the **largest** such survey. Its public value includes: evidence base for the ~$850M/year Title V block grant and its state needs assessments; free, public, annual data (most national child health surveys like NHIS lack state-level detail, while school-based surveys miss ages 0–4); the only routine state-level estimates on children with special health care needs; democratized access via the DRC for non-statisticians; and rich family/community context (ACEs, neighborhood, family resilience) unavailable in administrative claims data.

## 8. Preservationist's Risk Assessment

- **Single-vendor dependencies**: pre-2016 data lives only at CDC/NCHS SLAITS pages; the DRC (a nonprofit, CAHMI) is the only place the constructed indicator datasets and user-friendly query exist. Note the DRC's apparent domain migration (childhealthdata.org → nschdata.org) and its warning that 2016–2019 DRC datasets use superseded weights — old DRC downloads may not match current Census PUFs.
- **Version churn**: annual content revisions, a major 2016 series break, and re-issued 2016–2019 weights mean any archived analysis must be pinned to a specific file vintage.
- **Political/operational risk**: the survey depends on annual OMB ICR renewals and HRSA/CDC/USDA funding; the October–November 2025 shutdown materially disrupted the 2025 collection cycle. Periodic proposals to cut or restructure HHS data programs are a standing risk worth monitoring via the Federal Register and reginfo.gov ICR docket (0607-0990).
- **Current status (as of this research)**: active and healthy — 2025 PUFs are released, 2026 collection is cleared, and the ICR runs through mid-2029.

## Key Sources

Census Bureau NSCH program page and 2016–2025 methodology reports/FAQs; HRSA MCHB NSCH pages (including the participants FAQ confirming the Title 13 §8(b) / Title 42 §701(a)(2) authority); CRS reports R48088 and R42428 on the Title V Block Grant; NCBI Bookshelf NSCH data briefs on Title V measures; the DRC/CAHMI site; and OMB ICR package 0607-0990 at reginfo.gov.

## Current Status Snapshot (as of this research, October 2026)

Before applying the rubric, the operational facts: the NSCH is **alive and current**. The 2025 PUFs were released in October 2026; the 2026 cycle is cleared (ICR 202603-0607-004, OMB No. 0607-0990, approved with change June 16, 2026, expiring June 30, 2029, at a documented annual cost to the federal government of $9.7M); all PUFs back to 2016 remain downloadable from census.gov; pre-2016 SLAITS-era data remain at NCHS; and the HRSA/MCHB and CAHMI/DRC dissemination sites are live. However, the survey sits inside two agencies that have been severely disrupted, and one content removal has already been documented.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** All NSCH public use files (screener + topical, 2016–2025) remain posted at census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/data/datasets.html; the 2024 cycle data release page and October 2026 release of 2025 data confirm the archive is growing, not shrinking. Pre-2016 NSCH and NS-CSHCN data remain archived at CDC/NCHS. Census re-released all files since 2016 in April 2024 (revised weights) — a re-issue, not a removal. DRC enhanced datasets and the interactive query remain available.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The essentialdata.us Federal Data Terminations Tracker (last updated Aug. 17, 2026) lists the **NSCH under "Data Elements Removed"** (Agency: CENSUS, Type: Health): *"The survey continues; the item on unfair treatment because of sexual orientation or gender identity was removed, dropped without notice from the reposted 2024 questionnaire."* The supporting evidence is a Wayback Machine capture of the 2024 NSCH Topical Questionnaire T3 (archived Nov. 20, 2024, SOGI item present), the Williams Institute report *Removal of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity from Federal Data Collections: January 2025 to January 2026* (Feb. 2026), and the 2025 NSCH ICR revision. A questionnaire element that existed in a prior cycle was retroactively scrubbed from a reposted document with no notice — a documented alteration affecting prior-cycle materials.

**No evidence for High Risk or Gone:** No prior-year data file has been removed; the full microdata archive is intact.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** The historical microdata files themselves remain fully accessible and unaltered, but a data element present in a prior cycle's instrument was removed from reposted documentation without notice — this is precisely a "data element removed" event at the low end of the rubric, and the lack of notice is itself a preservation concern (undocumented retroactive edits to official instruments undermine the reliability of the record).

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** The 2026 ICR was approved with change on June 16, 2026 — a routine annual revision approved well before the prior expiration (5/31/2028); it runs through June 30, 2029. The 2025 PUF was released October 2026 and the 2026 collection is fielding. Publication cadence has not lapsed: 2024 data released December 2025; 2025 data released October 2026.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The 2025 cycle's collection was **materially delayed by the October 1–November 12, 2025 lapse in appropriations**: survey operations paused, mailings rescheduled, closeout extended from January 16 to March 6, 2026 (~7 weeks), and an extra $5 incentive mailing added to compensate (2025 NSCH Methodology Report). The Census Bureau's own assessment calls the two-month delay of the web partial follow-up test "a major setback." The 2024 cycle also slipped (closeout extended Jan. 10 → Feb. 7, 2025 after a National Processing Center mechanical failure; release in December 2025). These are "collection delayed" events under the rubric, even though publication dates were ultimately met.

**No evidence for High Risk/Gone:** No skipped collection, no missed statutory deadline, no ICR lapse; the survey survived the DOGE review of 100+ Census reimbursable surveys (see Policy).

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** The ICR is active and publications are roughly on schedule — the strongest parts of this category — but the 2025 collection was genuinely disrupted and extended by the shutdown, and the 2024–2025 cycles have both required closeout extensions. That is a realized, documented delay in collection, fitting "Moderate Risk," with an important mitigating factor that the pipeline has so far absorbed each shock.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for High Risk (by strict reading):** One documented reduction in granularity: the SOGI "unfair treatment" item was removed from the instrument (terminations tracker; Williams Institute), a presidential-action-driven content change. The 2025 shutdown disruption may also depress completed interviews/response rates for the 2025 file (the 2025 methodology report explicitly frames the incentive and schedule changes as compensation).

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The removal is a single content item; the core architecture is intact — annual frequency maintained (no skipped year since 2016), ~$9.7M annual budget and sample design unchanged (ICR burden essentially flat: 126,703 responses, 42,553 hours), state-level design retained, and the 2026 ICR shows ongoing methodological *investment* (incentive-envelope tests, web-partial follow-up experiments), not retrenchment. Publication timeliness preserved.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** None — an actual content element was removed, so this level is not available.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** Granularity, timeliness, and frequency are all *potentially or partially* affected but not broadly reduced: one item removed, one cycle's collection stretched, no change in sample size, frequency, geography, or mode. A strict reading ("any reduction in granularity = High") would score this High because of the SOGI item removal; I judge Moderate more proportionate because the reduction is confined to a single variable and every structural dimension of quality is otherwise maintained or improving. If further content items are removed in the 2026+ instruments, this should be re-rated High.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** The survey operates under explicitly named statutory authority — Title 13 U.S.C. §8(b), 42 U.S.C. §701(a)(2) (Title V authority), 42 U.S.C. §241, and 42 U.S.C. §1769d(a)(4)(B) — all cited on the ICR. It is the data backbone of the Title V MCH Block Grant ($850M+/year): source for 9 of 15 National Performance Measures, 7 of 25 National Outcome Measures, state five-year needs assessments required under §505(a), and 15 Healthy People 2030 objectives. No alternative collection can substitute — HRSA describes it as the only national *and* state-level survey of children's health.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The NSCH itself is not named or mandated in statute — Congress does not require this specific survey. Its existence depends on discretionary interagency funding (HRSA sponsorship via Title 13 §8(b) reimbursable agreements plus CDC/USDA supplements and state oversample purchases). It is "required for implementation" of Title V in practice but not in law; states could in principle assemble other sources (BRFSS child items, NHIS, YRBSS, state surveys), though none replicate the state-level 0–17 design.

**Evidence for High Risk:** Weak — programmatic use is extensive and documented, and no true substitute exists, so the "no known programmatic use / vague authorization / available substitutes" triggers are not met.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** The best fit is the rubric's middle level: not explicitly required by statute, but indispensable to implementing a federal program (Title V) with no adequate substitute. The strong, explicitly cited authorization and the survey's survival of the DOGE reimbursable-survey review (which killed surveys lacking clear sponsors/use) suggest the *practical* protection is stronger than the legal one.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk (collecting agency — Census Bureau):**
- Census has lost **1,300–1,500 employees since January 2025**, mostly via the deferred resignation program (AFGE Council 241 via Bloomberg Law; GovExec; workforce was ~13,230 in Sept. 2024) — exceeding the rubric's 1,000-staff threshold.
- ASA's *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025* estimates a **~15% staffing loss since FY24** and a FY26 request 9% below FY24 (with a 27% cut to periodic censuses/programs).
- **Leadership removed**: career Deputy Director Ron Jarmin was replaced as acting Director by Trump political appointee George Cook on Sept. 19, 2025 (CBPP), after Director Robert Santos's earlier departure — "leadership instability" the ASA calls unprecedented.
- ~100 additional RIF notices issued during the October 2025 shutdown; hiring constrained to 1-for-4 replacement (Federal News Network); >3,000-request contract approval backlog (Commerce policy) early in 2025.

**Evidence for High Risk (sponsoring agency — HRSA/MCHB):**
- HHS restructuring (March 27, 2025, per EO 14210) cut the department from 82,000 to 62,000 FTEs and folds HRSA into the new Administration for a Healthy America.
- HRSA lost **~25% of staff (700+ workers) between February and July 2025** (KFF Health News); **MCHB lost 20% of its employees**, and MCHB leader Michael Warren left in June 2025 (Gillibrand letter; CBS/KFF).
- The President's FY26 budget **proposes eliminating HRSA as an agency**, cutting Title V SPRANS by $46.7M, and eliminating adjacent child-health programs (Healthy Start, EMSC, EHDI-HRSA) (Fierce Healthcare; AMCHP).

**Mitigating evidence:** The NSCH's own funding is demonstrably intact — the 2026 ICR documents $9.7M/year and an approved 2026 collection — and both the 2024 and 2025 cycles were completed and published despite the disruption.

**Verdict: High Risk.** Both the collector and the sponsor meet multiple High thresholds simultaneously: Census lost well over 1,000 staff with leadership removed; HRSA lost ~25% of staff with MCHB leadership departed; and the sponsor agency's continued existence is proposed for elimination. The survey's dedicated funding has so far been spared, which is why this is High rather than a termination scenario.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Presidential-action-driven content change (realized):** The SOGI "unfair treatment" item was removed from the NSCH under Executive Order 14168 (the gender-ideology EO), documented by the Williams Institute's February 2026 report and logged in the essentialdata.us terminations tracker under "Data Elements Removed" — dropped "without notice" from the reposted 2024 questionnaire. This is exactly the rubric's "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities" affecting what data is collected. Comparable child/maternal-health surveys fared worse: **PRAMS** national weighting/publication suspended (CDC), **YRBSS** and **BRFSS** SOGI items removed, the **Violence Against Children and Youth Survey** terminated.
- **DOGE survey review:** DOGE declared five Census-conducted reimbursable surveys "terminated" in May 2025 and said it was reviewing 100+ more "one-by-one," with the GSA "Survey of Surveys" form warning of "ADVERSE ACTIONS, INCLUDING TERMINATION" for non-participation (AP; OPB/NPR). The NSCH is precisely this kind of survey (Census fielding for a sponsor agency), and while it survived into 2026 with an approved ICR, the review framework remains a standing, Administration-driven threat to reimbursable surveys.
- **HHS restructuring into AHA** (HRSA dissolved into a new entity) is a significant Administration-priority reorganization of the sponsor that creates uncertainty about MCHB's future stewardship of the survey.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The 2026 content revisions were processed through the normal PRA channel with public comment (60-day notice 90 FR 56128, Dec. 5, 2025; 30-day notice 91 FR 14523, Mar. 25, 2026), and the survey's core mission (child health, Title V measurement) is not on its face a target of "Make America Healthy Again" priorities — indeed chronic-disease/child-health framing could favor it.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** None available — changes since January 2025 have occurred.

**Verdict: High Risk.** A presidential-action-driven content removal has already happened (EO 14168/SOGI item), the survey sits in the exact category (Census reimbursable survey) targeted by DOGE's terminations, and its sponsor is being dissolved into a new entity. That said, the survey's survival of the 2025–2026 review cycle and its Title V constituency are meaningful counterweights.

---

## Caveats on Sources

- Web-search capacity was exhausted mid-research; I could not verify the final FY2026 appropriations outcome for HRSA/AHA or examine the full 2026 questionnaire content-revision document, either of which could sharpen the Policy and Data Quality ratings.
- The HRSA participants FAQ page returned HTTP 403; the federal staffing tracker (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) is a JavaScript application whose data couldn't be parsed here and is itself being archived after Dec. 31, 2025 — but the underlying staffing figures are corroborated by AFGE, ASA, KFF Health News, and GovExec reporting cited above.
- The USAJobs tracker measures *job postings*, not hires or separations; direct staff-loss figures come from the journalistic and ASA sources.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: Moderate Risk** — all data files 2016–2025 (and pre-2016 at NCHS) remain fully accessible, but one data element (the SOGI unfair-treatment item) was removed without notice from a reposted prior-cycle questionnaire.

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk** — ICR active through June 2029 and 2025/2026 data published or fielding on schedule, but the 2025 collection was delayed and extended ~7 weeks by the government shutdown, and both recent cycles required closeout extensions.

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk** — annual frequency, sample design, and state-level granularity are maintained, but one content item has actually been removed (a literal reading would score this High) and the shutdown disrupted the 2025 collection.

**Statutory Context: Moderate Risk** — not mandated by statute, but operating under explicitly named authority (13 U.S.C. §8(b); 42 U.S.C. §701(a)(2)) and indispensable, with no substitute, to Title V Block Grant implementation.

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk** — Census Bureau lost 1,300–1,500 staff (~15%) with leadership replaced; HRSA lost ~25% of staff, MCHB ~20% with leadership departed; the President's FY26 budget proposes eliminating HRSA entirely — though NSCH's own $9.7M/year funding is currently intact.

**Policy: High Risk** — an EO 14168-driven data element removal has already occurred; DOGE terminated five Census reimbursable surveys and reviewed 100+ more, of which NSCH is one type; and the sponsoring agency is being restructured out of existence, though the survey itself survived the 2025–2026 review cycle.

**Overall read:** The NSCH is a functioning survey with strong statutory anchoring through the Title V program that has so far survived an extraordinarily hostile environment for federal data collection. The primary live risks are not outright termination but (a) incremental, politically driven content erosion, (b) the fragility of its two host institutions, and (c) shutdown-driven operational delays. For preservation purposes, the highest-value actions would be archiving each year's questionnaire PDFs and codebooks at time of release (given the documented retroactive scrubbing of the 2024 instrument) and maintaining redundant copies of the pre-2016 NCHS-hosted archive.
